description: Ground Truth talks from BSides Las Vegas 2022.

talks.title: Security AI in the real world
talks.teaser: Looks at how AI is applied to security work in practical settings.

talks.title: That Escalated Quickly: A System for Alert Prioritization
talks.teaser: Presents a system for prioritizing security alerts so the most urgent ones get escalated first.

talks.title: GPT-3 and me
talks.teaser: Shows how large language models like GPT-3 can describe command lines and detect spam from only a few examples.
talks.summary:
The talk, given by two data scientists from Sophos, argues that very large self-supervised models are changing what machine learning can do, and that security researchers should work out how such models fit defensive problems. The speakers explain self-supervised training, where a model learns from unlabeled data by solving an artificial prediction task, and show how capability grows with model size. GPT-3 is too large to run on ordinary hardware, so the work relies on API access and its cost.

The middle of the talk turns to experiments. One demonstration translates obfuscated malicious command lines into plain-English descriptions that analysts could use to speed triage. Output improved when signature names from detection rules were added to the prompt, and the team picked the best candidate by generating a command back from each description and comparing it to the original. A second experiment classifies spam messages from only a handful of labeled examples through in-context learning, reaching roughly 90 to 95 percent accuracy, while a random forest baseline barely beat guessing. Fine-tuning on around a thousand samples pushed accuracy higher but made inference too slow for routine use.

The closing message is that few-shot prompting can produce a usable prototype quickly, but cost and latency restrict it to selective use, such as on alerts that already look suspicious. The speakers also floated translating natural-language questions into database queries and suggesting command completions for analysts as areas to explore.

talks.title: Back to Basics: Using Descriptive Statistics to Study the Shape of the Internet
talks.teaser: Shows how descriptive statistics and exploratory analysis of internet-wide scan data reveal patterns in exposed services and risks.
talks.summary:
Emily Austin uses descriptive statistics to explore internet-wide scan data. She opens with the case for exploratory analysis before building models, using the classic Anscombe's quartet example to show how identical summary numbers can hide very different data shapes.

The middle of the talk applies these methods to the internet itself. Counting services by port and protocol, HTTP dominates the observed services, while SSH and FTP mostly run on their assigned ports, with a notable cluster of FTP on an unusual port. Cloud providers host many services, yet only a small share of exposed services sit in the major clouds. Looking at SSH software versions and ciphers shows deprecated algorithms still in active use, along with implausible version strings that may be broken, hacked or deliberately misleading. Risk data from passive scanning groups findings into misconfigurations, exposures and vulnerabilities, with misconfigurations forming the largest share. Patch curves for the Log4j, GitLab and Confluence vulnerabilities differ sharply, showing how quickly each one was addressed.

The closing section looks at the long tail of distributions, where anomalous entries can reveal unusual or broken systems. The takeaway for practitioners is that understanding data before modeling it leads to better questions, and that simple aggregate views can help non-specialists prioritize work amid alert fatigue.

talks.title: Making InfoSec Better Through Library Science
talks.teaser: Draws lessons from library science to show how security teams can communicate better and support their users.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a short audience exercise about good and bad memories of libraries, then contrasts libraries' generally positive reputation with the often poor reception security teams receive. A brief history of library science follows, from early guidance on building libraries through the founding of the Library of Congress, along with a reminder that classification systems can carry bias and need ongoing correction.

The middle section makes the case for a shared security vocabulary. The speaker argues the industry needs a diverse, authoritative body to settle terms, since jargon and competing labels for the same threat confuse users, journalists and executives alike. The speaker then adapts the five laws of library science into a draft set of principles for information security: security should be accessible to everyone, teams should curate what is in their environment, education should reach every person, guidance should be kept current, and it should be tailored to different audiences.

Toward the end, the talk introduces the reference interview, a multi-step library practice for finding out what a patron actually needs. Examples include a user who reported a routine newsletter every day because of a misunderstanding, and an employee whose account was compromised after a phishing attempt. The takeaways are to make the security team approachable, listen for what users leave unsaid, ask specific follow-up questions, document outcomes, and verify that fixes keep working. Security is presented as a human problem that needs to evolve with the organization.

talks.title: Lessons learned while modeling rare catastrophic cyber loss events
talks.teaser: Explains how catastrophe models quantify rare, widespread cyber losses using causal simulation rather than standard statistics.
talks.summary:
The speakers, from RMS, a company that builds catastrophe models mostly for insurers and reinsurers, frame cyber risk as a portfolio problem. They separate attritional losses, which hit single organizations, from tail events that strike many firms at once, and show how both feed into an insurance premium calculation.

Their central argument is that frequency and severity statistics cannot estimate extreme events that have never been observed. Instead, their model builds a synthetic world of firms, software, vulnerabilities and threat actors linked by causal mechanisms, then runs it across tens of thousands of simulated years. The talk also covers fitting probability distributions to data, how the addressable population of an attack and chains of required vulnerabilities shape worm-style losses, and data gaps such as short usable time series and sparse incident reporting.

The rarest modeled events, roughly one-in-a-hundred per year, are most likely driven by wormable exploits or supply chain attacks on large vendors, with wipers as the probable payload. Audience questions covered insider threats, which the current model does not include, and whether the approach suits a single firm. The takeaway is that uncertainty in cyber will stay greater than in natural hazards, so expert judgment has to complement any such model.

talks.title: Attack Flow: From Data Points to Data Paths
talks.teaser: Shows how attack paths can be stored as graph data so attacker actions and affected assets can be queried together.
talks.summary:
Gabriel Bassett traces the idea back to a government risk assessment where spreadsheet scoring and five-by-five matrices failed to explain why analysts disagreed. Writing out the reasoning revealed that the real content was attack paths: sequences of attacker actions against assets, each with an effect. He presents Attack Flow, a schema built around actions, assets, properties, relationships and flows, which lets those paths be stored as graph data.

The middle of the talk surveys common security data, including red team reports, attack simulation code, signatures, threat intelligence feeds, incident response notes and budget lists. Most of it is flat text, weakly linked, or aggregated in ways that hide context. Bassett converts sample red team and incident data into Attack Flow, loads it into a graph database, and queries it for compromised assets and frequent actions. He also explains how the same path can be read from red or blue team perspectives, and how mitigations can be assessed as a group against a path rather than one vulnerability at a time.

He closes with possible extensions: modeling normal behavior, mapping blast radius between systems, linking external threat actor data, and using link prediction to suggest steps an investigation may have missed. He points attendees to the public schema and converter repositories, noting that the project is new and still needs tooling and training.

talks.title: Weeding Out Living-off-the-land Attacks at Scale
talks.teaser: Shows how a machine learning detector for living-off-the-land command lines is built, labeled, and tuned to avoid alert floods.
talks.summary:
The speakers describe building a machine learning system that flags living-off-the-land binary attacks, where legitimate system tools are abused through malicious command lines. The goal was to surface attacks that existing detections miss without flooding a security operations center with false positives. Command lines were the chosen signal, and with roughly 1.5 billion invocations per day the data volume was not the obstacle. Getting trustworthy labels was.

To build labels, the team combined past incident results, indirect labels borrowed from file and URL verdicts and sandbox reports, and rules written by threat analysts as allow and block lists. They split training, validation and test data by time so the model was scored on command lines it had never seen. A gradient-boosted baseline using character-transition features was compared with two convolutional neural networks. The first models looked accurate, but a daily replay of a one percent sample showed hundreds of alerts. The speakers used this to illustrate the base rate fallacy: when malicious events are rare, even a very accurate classifier produces mostly false positives.

The fix was guardrails. The model only matters when analyst rules fire. Block-list matches alert directly, while suspicious or debatable rule matches alert only when the model scores them highly. The reported results showed a manageable number of daily alerts, a true positive rate near 0.9 to 1 over several weeks, and some detections the existing system did not make. The takeaway is that standalone ML rarely works on skewed security data, and that data engineering and ongoing analyst feedback matter as much as the model itself.

talks.title: Repurposing Vulnerability Tickets to Predict Severity Levels
talks.teaser: Shows how natural language vulnerability tickets can be classified with machine learning to predict their severity levels.

talks.title: Model Robustness Isn't Security
talks.teaser: Argues that adversarial robustness is a poor fit for security, and lays out the defenses that matter for ML systems.
talks.summary:
Sven Cattell argues that model robustness, the idea that a classifier stays correct for every input within a small distance of a sample, should not be treated as a security property. He separates the popular meaning of adversarial examples from the mathematical definition practitioners use, then explains how checking every point in that neighborhood becomes unmanageable as input dimensionality grows. Using MNIST as a running example, he estimates how many inputs would need checking even for small perturbation radii, and argues that adversarial training and Lipschitz constraints only partly address the problem.

The middle of the talk covers the trade-offs and real-world bypasses. Robust models can lose substantial accuracy, and for malware classifiers a small false-positive rate matters more than robustness. He describes a production malware model whose false-negative rate spiked months after release because a malware family found a bypass, a problem that robustness would not have prevented. He also walks through older attacks, including spam filters defeated by padding and obfuscation, and an allowlist-style malware detector that was bypassed through its handling of game anti-cheat software.

For the closing takeaways, he recommends basic hygiene first: validating inputs, scanning dependencies, avoiding pickle for untrusted models, hardening pipelines and securing storage such as S3 buckets. He then urges protecting training data as the most valuable asset, layering defenses around the model, monitoring deployed models for drift, modeling realistic attackers, and changing features over time. He also stresses responding quickly when a model fails.
